newsitem.title: USA: Anchorage mayor says city's future is bright.
newsitem.headline: Anchorage mayor says city's future is bright.

text.p: Anchorage in the next few years will reap benefits from Alaska's new oil development and growth in the air cargo and tourism industries, Mayor Rick Mystrom said Monday.

Alaska's largest city could also become a commercial fisheries centre, taking some business from Seattle, if it developed a seafood processing industry, Mystrom told the Anchorage Chamber of Commerce.

For now, fishing industry traffic runs directly from Unalaska/Dutch Harbour, the Aleutian city that is the nation's top seafood port, and Seattle, he said. Anchorage, lacking seafood processors, offers no incentive for fish-laden vessels to stop on their way from the booming seafood port, he said.

That may change with the completion of the $125 million Alaska Seafood International plant in Anchorage, the mayor said. Construction of the plant, to process and package Alaska fish, began two weeks ago.

Mystrom said he hoped the seafood plant, financed by the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority and Taiwan's Central Investment Holding Co., will help spread some of the Aleutian economic boom to Anchorage.
"Dutch Harbour is kind of the Hong Kong of America, and Anchorage could benefit greatly if we were the support centre," he said.
The city's air cargo business will be enhanced by more traffic from such carriers as Korea Air Lines and United Air Lines, Mystrom said.
Meanwhile, five new hotels are under construction in Anchorage to take advantage of the growing tourist trade, he said. A sixth hotel is being planned for the centre of Anchorage, he said.
The city has little control over oil development, Mystrom conceded.
"What we can do is continue to make Anchorage the kind of place (where) people in the petroleum industry want to live and want to work," he said.
To that end, the city should continue work to reduce its crime rate, which fell by 31 percent from mid-1995 to mid-1997, Mystrom said.
One of his goals is to get approval from the state legislature for a new jail in central Anchorage to replace the overcrowded existing building.
The existing jail held an average of 136 inmates a day during the past fiscal year, he said. Its emergency capacity is 108 inmates, he said.
"If we want to continue the declining crime rate through the year 2000, we have to have a replacement jail, we have to have more jail beds," he said.
